text:
Step seven, normalize: every fact in one place. Except this design copies one fact, on purpose. Products holds the price today. Order items holds the price charged, back then. Ana bought two mugs at ten dollars. The mug costs twelve now. Total her order from its lines, and it's forty-four dollars, what she paid. Total it from today's prices, and it says forty-eight. History would quietly rewrite itself. That's step eight: walk real rows through the design, and see what breaks.

But a design is never done. A task tracker starts with just tasks. Then people want due dates. Then projects, labels, a history. That's not failure. It's the product learning about the world. The catch? A live schema has rows, code, reports and tests leaning on its shape... and people's habits, too.

Say every task now needs a priority. Add it as required, in one step... and Postgres refuses. The tasks already there have no priority, so the rule would be broken the moment it existed. So go in steps. Add the column empty. Backfill the old rows, here with normal. Check that none is missing. Then make it required. That backfill is a design decision, by the way. It says what the old rows MEAN.

Bigger changes work the same way. Say a task's one owner has to become a team of assignees. First, expand: add the new table beside the old column, so both shapes work. Move the data across, then the code. Only once nothing reads the old column... contract, and remove it.
